The WHO estimates that over one billion people currently require one or more assistive products, with the majority being older adults and individuals with disabilities. This number is expected to exceed two billion by 2050 due to aging populations and the increasing prevalence of non-communicable diseases. However, only one in ten people in need currently have access to assistive technology. Lack of access often leads to exclusion, poverty, and isolation, exacerbating the impact of disease and disability on individuals, families, and society. To address this gap, WHO established the Global Cooperation on Assistive Health Technology (GATE) initiative, prioritizing research and innovation. A core group of experts was formed to identify strategic research priorities, culminating in a GATE Research Group meeting in Budapest in September 2015. Experts from various organizations and countries contributed to the development of a global priority research agenda aimed at improving access to high-quality, affordable assistive technology. The research agenda focuses on five thematic areas: 1. The effects, costs, and economic impact of assistive technology. 2. Policies, systems, service provision models, and best practices. 3. Development of high-quality and affordable assistive technology. 4. Capacity building and human resource deployment for assistive technology services. 5. Standards and methodologies for assessing assistive technology needs and unmet needs. The agenda emphasizes user involvement in all aspects of research, particularly in policy and service provision, and adopts a social and environmental model of disability and participation. The report aims to share the global priority research agenda and encourage stakeholders to support research activities that close the gap between global assistive technology needs and unmet needs. Assistive technology encompasses products, systems, and services designed to maintain or improve functioning and promote well-being. It enables individuals with functional difficulties to lead healthy, productive, independent, and dignified lives, participating in education, employment, and social activities. Assistive products are essential for compensating for impairments, reducing the consequences of functional decline, minimizing the need for caregivers, and rationalizing health and welfare costs. WHO estimates that over one billion people could benefit from assistive products, with this number expected to rise above two billion by 2050 due to aging populations and the increasing prevalence of non-communicable diseases. Aging is associated with a gradual decline in physical and mental capacity and an increased risk of disease, though these changes are not linear or consistent. Those most in need of assistive technology include individuals with disabilities, older adults, people with non-communicable diseases, and those with mental health conditions such as dementia and autism. Despite the growing need, only 10% of people in need currently have access to assistive technology due to barriers such as high costs, lack of financing, limited availability, insufficient awareness, and a shortage of trained personnel. For example, while 70 million people require wheelchairs, only 5–15% have access to one. Similarly, hearing aid production meets only 10% of global needs and 3% of needs in low-income countries. Addressing this gap is an urgent global priority to prevent further marginalization and ensure access to quality assistive technology, enabling individuals to be productive and enjoy fundamental human rights. The United Nations (UN) recognizes poor access to assistive technology as a critical issue. The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities entitles all individuals to accessible and affordable assistive technology and mandates states to take effective measures to ensure access. Increasing access to high-quality and affordable medical products, including assistive products, is one of WHO’s six leadership priorities. In response, WHO launched the GATE initiative in 2014 to improve access to high-quality, affordable assistive products as part of its commitment to essential, safe, effective, and affordable medical products. To achieve this goal, GATE developed a global priority research agenda through a comprehensive consultation and consensus process. This agenda was created through six steps: 1. An online questionnaire to identify potential global research priorities. 2. A GATE Research Group consensus meeting with key stakeholders. 3. A follow-up meeting to consolidate research themes. 4. Drafting an initial priority research agenda. 5. Peer review and feedback. 6. Finalization of the global priority research agenda. Experts from all WHO regions participated in the process, contributing diverse perspectives. The online questionnaire received 50 responses, with input from high-, middle-, and low-income countries. Despite efforts, responses from lowand middle-income countries were limited, reflecting the current status of access to assistive technology. The GATE Research Group consensus meeting, held in Budapest in September 2015, involved 64 experts from 25 countries. Participants included researchers, occupational therapists, physical therapists, and users of assistive products. The meeting featured presentations and focus group discussions on four broad research themes, generating diverse ideas and opinions for further analysis. A follow-up meeting with 16 participants from 11 countries refined the research themes into a condensed set of priority areas. The core group categorized 256 research suggestions into five thematic areas, forming the basis of the initial draft research agenda. Feedback from participants validated the thematic areas and provided constructive comments for improvement. The finalized global priority research agenda focuses on the five thematic areas, aiming to guide research efforts that address the substantial gap between the need for and provision of assistive technology.
